metadata.note: Passenger rail to Dolgeville, NY -- a Herkimer County village that had no railroad at all until its own industrialist built one. Alfred Dolge, the felt and piano-sounding-board manufacturer the village is named for, was the principal shareholder behind the Little Falls and Dolgeville Railroad, incorporated 1891/1892 to connect his mills to the New York Central main line and the Erie Canal at Little Falls. The first train ran December 14 1892 and the line was complete by December 31 1893, 10.8 miles built for $539,430.56, running east from Little Falls along the Mohawk and then north up the East Canada Creek valley past Manheim Center and Ingham Mills. Passengers were carried from the start: the first summer saw heavy excursion traffic to High Falls Park in flatcars rebuilt as open cars, 25 cents round trip from the Little Falls depot. The NYC&HR bought the road July 24 1906 for $382,687.72 and consolidated it April 16 1913, when it became simply the Dolgeville Branch; NYC integrated operations fully in 1917. North of Dolgeville, the Dolgeville and Salisbury Railway -- organised July 8 1907 by the Salisbury Steel and Iron Company, construction begun December 1906, 3.89 miles to the iron mines at Irondale via Salisbury Center -- was an ore road that also carried passengers, and was operated from the outset by the (NYC-owned) LF&D. Passenger service to Salisbury Center ended in 1925; passenger service on the entire line ended April 30 1933. Freight lasted far longer -- the last train over the branch ran July 15 1964 behind a 600 hp switcher -- but per the passenger-only rule nothing here is drawn past 1933.

not_yet_sourced: SOURCE CONFLICT -- when the Dolgeville-Salisbury Center trackage was built. The Little Falls Historical Society describes the original 10.8-mile 1893 line as running 'east from Little Falls, passing Manheim Center, then on to Ingham Mills, then heading north on to Dolgeville, then continuing on to go farther north to Salisbury Center, where it stopped at the northern terminal' -- i.e. Salisbury Center reached in 1893. Gino's Rail Page and Penney/KC Jones instead date the whole Dolgeville-Irondale line (Salisbury Center is a station on it) to the Dolgeville & Salisbury Railway of 1907, built December 1906 onward and opened 1908. This file follows the latter, because those two accounts give specific dates, a specific promoter (Salisbury Steel and Iron Co.) and a mileage (3.89) that matches the traced railbed exactly. If the Historical Society is right, the Dolgeville-Salisbury Center portion should start in 1893, not 1908, and should carry LF&D company/colour for 1893-1906.

SOURCE CONFLICT -- opening date of the Dolgeville & Salisbury. Gino's Rail Page says the extension opened April 1908; another account has it 'reported as completed September 1, 1909'. 1908 is used here.
The 10.8-mile figure for the LF&D main line is 1.4 mi longer than the traced railbed (9.41 mi); the endpoints the original measurement used are not documented. See geometry_quality.
No timetable was found for either line. Every headway_min value in this file is an estimate -- see each segment note.

metadata.colour_policy: Rule 4 split. The LF&D is drawn in its own colour only for 1892-1906, its independent years; from the NYC&HR purchase of July 24 1906 the same railbed is redrawn as a second feature in the New York Central colour #5C677D used repo-wide, because from that date the New York Central owned the road that ran the trains. (The 1913 consolidation and the 1917 operational integration are recorded as segment boundaries inside the NYC feature rather than as a colour change.) The Dolgeville-Irondale extension is NYC-coloured for its whole life: it was corporately the Dolgeville & Salisbury Railway until 1913, but it was operated from opening by the LF&D, which the NYC already owned, so no year of it was ever run by an independent company.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap: every point comes from the curated OSM route relation 1376437 'Dolgeville Branch' (source:name = 1917 Moody's Manual), whose member ways are tagged railway=abandoned, name='Little Falls and Dolgeville Railroad', old_railway_operator=NYC. No straight-line approximation anywhere in this feature. Traced length 15.14 km (9.41 mi) against a documented 10.8 miles for the LF&D main line -- the 1.4-mile shortfall is most likely measurement endpoints, not a wrong alignment: the trace stops at the junction with the NYC main line east of Little Falls (43.0426, -74.8479), about 0.75 mi short of the Little Falls passenger station, and the north end is cut at the documented D&S junction rather than at the far end of the Dolgeville yard. The alignment is the abandoned railbed itself, contemporary with the era drawn -- not a later relocation.

segments.note: Incorporated 1891/1892 with Alfred Dolge -- the felt and piano-material manufacturer the village is named for -- as principal shareholder, to link his Dolgeville mills to the New York Central main line and the Erie Canal at Little Falls. First train December 14 1892; line complete December 31 1893, 10.8 miles at a cost of $539,430.56. Passenger-carrying from the first season: heavy 1893 excursion traffic to High Falls Park in flatcars rebuilt as open cars, 25 cents round trip from the Little Falls depot. Frequency estimated, unsourced -- no LF&D timetable was found; 240 minutes stands for roughly four round trips a day, typical of a branch of this length.

segments.note: Consolidated into the New York Central and Hudson River Railroad April 16 1913 and renamed the Dolgeville Branch; NYC took complete control of branch operations in 1917. Passenger service on the entire line ceased April 30 1933 -- the last drawn year. Freight continued long afterwards; the last train over the branch ran July 15 1964 behind a 600 hp switcher, but no passengers rode it, so nothing is drawn after 1933. Frequency estimated, unsourced.

properties.geometry_quality: Real-traced from OpenStreetMap, same relation 1376437; the Dolgeville-Salisbury Center portion survives as the 'Salisbury & Dolgeville Greenway Trail' rail-trail and the rest as railway=abandoned. No straight-line approximation. Traced length 6.27 km (3.89 mi) against the documented 3.89 miles Dolgeville-Irondale -- an exact match, which is what fixes the split point between this feature and the LF&D main line at (43.1133, -74.7722), 1.4 km north of Dolgeville village centre. Passes within 150 m of Salisbury Center and ends within 100 m of Irondale.

segments.note: Dolgeville and Salisbury Railway, organised July 8 1907 by the Salisbury Steel and Iron Company to reach its iron mines at Irondale, 3.89 miles north of Dolgeville via Salisbury Center. Construction began December 1906; opened April 1908 (one account instead reports completion September 1 1909). Built for ore, but it carried passengers too, and was operated from the start by the Little Falls & Dolgeville -- by then New York Central property, which is why this feature carries NYC colour for its whole life. Frequency estimated, unsourced -- 480 minutes stands for roughly two round trips a day on a short mixed-train branch.
